questions.solution:
$\text{speed} = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$, measured in m/s.

**Velocity** is speed with a direction, which is why an object going round a circle at a steady rate has constant speed but changing velocity.

questions.q: An object continues at constant velocity unless acted on by:
questions.solution:
Newton's first law: only a **resultant** (unbalanced) force changes an object's motion.

Balanced forces produce no change at all — a car at steady speed has its engine's drive exactly cancelled by friction and drag.

questions.q: The equation relating force, mass and acceleration is:
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{F = ma}$.

For a given force, a heavier object accelerates less. Mass is a measure of how strongly an object **resists** being accelerated, which is what inertia means.

questions.q: The principle of conservation of energy states that energy:
questions.solution:
Energy is **transferred** between stores, never created or destroyed.

'Wasted' energy has not vanished — it has usually spread out as heat into the surroundings, where it is too dilute to be useful.
options: cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred

questions.q: The moment of a force about a pivot is:
questions.solution:
$\text{moment} = \text{force} \times \text{perpendicular distance from the pivot}$, in N m.

A long spanner needs less force for the same turning effect, which is why they are made long.

questions.q: A car travels $150$ m in $10$ s. Find its average speed, in m/s.
A car accelerates from $5$ m/s to $25$ m/s in $4$ s. Find its acceleration, in m/s$^{2}$.
Find the force (in N) needed to give a $60$ kg mass an acceleration of $2$ m/s$^{2}$.
Find the kinetic energy (in J) of a $2$ kg object moving at $10$ m/s.
questions.solution:
$E_{k} = \tfrac12 mv^{2} = \tfrac12 \times 2 \times 100 = \mathbf{100}$ J.

Kinetic energy goes as the **square** of the speed, which is why doubling a car's speed quadruples its braking distance.

questions.q: A force of $20$ N acts $0.4$ m from a pivot. Find the moment, in N m.
State Newton's three laws of motion and give an everyday example of each.
questions.solution:
**First law (inertia).** An object stays at rest, or moves at constant velocity, unless a **resultant force** acts on it.

**Example:** passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes — they carry on at the old speed until the seat belt stops them.

**Second law.** The acceleration is proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to the mass: $F = ma$.

**Example:** an empty shopping trolley is easy to get moving; the same push barely shifts a full one.

**Third law.** For every action there is an **equal and opposite reaction**, acting on a **different** body.

**Example:** a rocket pushes gas backwards, and the gas pushes the rocket forwards. Walking works the same way — you push the ground back, it pushes you forward.

**The crucial detail of the third law:** the two forces act on **different objects**, which is why they do not cancel out. If both acted on the same body, nothing could ever accelerate.

questions.q: Describe the energy transfers in a swinging pendulum and in a falling ball, and explain why the pendulum eventually stops.
questions.solution:
**Pendulum.**

• At the **highest point** of the swing: all **gravitational potential energy**, and momentarily at rest.

• **Swinging down:** potential $\to$ **kinetic**.

• At the **lowest point:** maximum kinetic energy, maximum speed, minimum potential.

• **Swinging up the other side:** kinetic $\to$ potential.

The cycle repeats, with energy shuttling back and forth.

**Falling ball.** Potential $\to$ kinetic, so it speeds up as it falls. On impact, the kinetic energy becomes sound and heat, plus some elastic energy if the ball bounces.

**Why the pendulum stops.** **Air resistance and friction at the pivot** transfer a little energy to the surroundings as heat and sound on every swing.

The total energy is unchanged — conservation still holds — but it has spread out into the air and the support, where it is far too dilute to move the pendulum.

**This is the real meaning of 'wasted' energy:** not destroyed, but dissipated. In a vacuum with a frictionless pivot the pendulum would swing forever, which is exactly what makes a pendulum clock's escapement necessary — it returns the small amount lost on each swing.

questions.q: Explain what the gradient and the area represent on a distance-time graph and on a speed-time graph, and describe the motion shown by a horizontal line on each.
questions.solution:
**Distance-time graph.**

• **Gradient = speed.** A steep line means fast; a shallow line means slow.

• A **straight** line means constant speed; a **curve** means changing speed.

• The **area** under it has no physical meaning.

• A **horizontal line** means the distance is not changing — the object is **stationary**.

**Speed-time graph.**

• **Gradient = acceleration.** A positive gradient is speeding up, negative is slowing down.

• **Area under the graph = distance travelled.** This is the most useful single fact about these graphs.

• A **horizontal line** means constant speed — **zero acceleration**, not stationary.

**That difference is the classic confusion:** a horizontal line means 'not moving' on one graph and 'moving steadily' on the other. Always read the axis label first.

**Finding the area.** Split the shape into triangles and rectangles. For constant acceleration from rest to $20$ m/s in $10$ s, the area is a triangle: $\tfrac12 \times 10 \times 20 = 100$ m.

**A line sloping down to the axis** on a speed-time graph shows deceleration to a stop — and the area under it is the braking distance.

questions.q: State the principle of moments, and calculate the force needed at one end of a $2$ m uniform plank pivoted at its centre to balance a $40$ N weight placed $0.5$ m from the pivot on the other side.
questions.solution:
**Principle of moments.** For a body in equilibrium, the **sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments** about that point.

**The calculation.** The pivot is at the centre, so each end is $1$ m from it. The plank is uniform, so its own weight acts **at the pivot** and has no moment.

**Clockwise moment** (the $40$ N weight at $0.5$ m):

$40 \times 0.5 = 20$ N m

**Anticlockwise moment** (the unknown force $F$ at $1$ m):

$F \times 1$

**Balancing:**

$F \times 1 = 20 \Rightarrow F = \mathbf{20}$ N.

**Worth noticing:** the force needed is only half the weight, because it acts at twice the distance. That is exactly how a lever multiplies force — and why a crowbar works.

**Two conditions for full equilibrium:** the moments must balance **and** the resultant force must be zero. Here the pivot supplies the extra $60$ N upwards.

questions.q: Define density and pressure, and calculate the pressure exerted by a $600$ N person standing on one foot of area $0.015$ m$^{2}$.
questions.solution:
**Density** $= \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}$, in kg/m$^{3}$ or g/cm$^{3}$.

It explains floating: an object floats if it is **less dense** than the fluid. A steel ship floats because its hull encloses a great deal of air, making its **average** density less than water's.

**Pressure** $= \dfrac{\text{force}}{\text{area}}$, in pascals (N/m$^{2}$).

**The calculation:**

$P = \dfrac{600}{0.015} = \mathbf{40\,000}$ Pa $= 40$ kPa.

**On two feet** the area doubles and the pressure halves, to $20$ kPa.

**Why area matters so much.** The same person in stiletto heels, with perhaps $0.0001$ m$^{2}$ of contact, exerts $6$ **MPa** — enough to dent a wooden floor.

The **force is the same in every case**; only the area changes. It is why snowshoes work, why a knife is sharpened, and why a camel's foot is broad.
